title: Cloud–Bulk Interaction Field Equations and the Geometric Origin of the Cosmological Parameter Λ
content: Observations from a wide range of cosmological probes indicate the presence of a non-zero cosmological constant, $\Lambda$, commonly interpreted as a constant vacuum energy density. In the standard framework combining General Relativity and quantum field theory, quantum vacuum contributions enter the gravitational field equations as terms proportional to $g_{\mu\nu}$. This produces the well-known discrepancy between the observationally inferred and theoretically predicted vacuum energy densities, referred to as the cosmological constant problem. In addition, recent analyses combining SNe~Ia, $H(z)$, BAO, LSS, BBN, and CMB datasets have reported evidence favoring a time-dependent cosmological parameter, with statistical significances reaching up to $4.2\,\sigma$ for certain dataset combinations. These findings motivate a re-examination of the assumption that $\Lambda$ represents a constant vacuum energy density. The presented framework instead treats the quantum vacuum as a dynamical background (Bulk) endowed with its own metric $\tilde g_{\mu\nu}$, while embedded astrophysical systems are described as localized manifolds (Clouds). The resulting interaction field equations reduce locally to the Einstein field equations in the fully synchronized Cloud--Bulk limit. In the unlocked cosmological regime, the equations demonstrate that the effective cosmological term emerges from the residual Cloud--Bulk synchronization, with the background Bulk curvature setting the characteristic geometric scale of the interaction. Complementary to alternative $\Lambda$CDM explanations of late-time cosmic acceleration (e.g., entropic or entanglement approaches), the framework provides an effective geometric description in which the small observed value of $\Lambda$ reflects the weakly curved geometry of the nearly flat present Universe, while remaining consistent with the preference of the observational constraints.
